deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three related notes, dated 1815 Aug. 16, on an instrument mounted equatorially (it has an hour circle and measures polar distance), set up at Göttingen.

(A) Horizon-obstruction survey, NW sky. The header reads 'Heliom.[?] in NW'; the word is uncertain. For polar distances p = 95°, 90°, 80°, 70°, 60°, 50° Gauss lists two western hour angles each:
- the first is when the objective 'fängt an frei zu werden' (begins to be free);
- the second is when it 'ist ganz frei' (is completely free).
The pairs are (4h50', 5h5½'), (4h30', 4h50'), (4h0½', 4h20'), (3h35', 3h48½'), (2h56½', 3h10½') and (2h23', 2h30').
A further sequence of hour angles is noted for obstructions:
- 4h16½'–6h24': impediment at the stand (Stativ);
- 9h58'–9h59½': chimney;
- 10h5½'–10h54': houses;
- a right-hand column 5h21', 5h51', 6h10½', 6h39', 8h16½', ending at 11h16' 'Ende'.
This is a table of the sky region usable from this station, given as (p, t). There is no derivation, only data.

(B) Hour-circle convention. Gauss states that the lower (northern) zero of the hour circle is the true one. Readings taken with the telescope on the west side must be increased by 12h if positive polar distances are used, and the opposite holds for negative ones. This is the usual 12h / sign flip of a German-type equatorial mount when the telescope is swung through the pole.

(C) Terrestrial mark. For the cross on the Jacobi church tower the instrument gave hour angle 12h + 6°48'15'' and polar distance 44°56'5''. Hours and degrees are mixed: whole hours plus degrees of arc. The next page lists a refined value of 12h 6°56'45'', 44°54'10'' under 'Lage gegen den Aequator'.

Consistency check (mine): with φ ≈ 51°32' and the tower's altitude about 6°44' (from the next page), a point near the northern meridian has p ≈ φ − h ≈ 44.8°. Its hour angle is about 12h plus a few degrees, which fits an azimuth about 4.5° from north. The tower thus serves as a fixed azimuth/index mark.

(D) Clock error from sun hour angles. The clock is evidently a sidereal clock. For four observations of the sun, Gauss has the measured hour angle t: 4h44'12'', 4h48'8'', 4h53'7'', 6h16'44''.
- Column 'Uhr voraus' (presumably clock reading minus hour angle): 9h54'0'', 9h54'1.7'', 9h54'2.9'', 9h54'22.5''.
- Column 'Mittag ohne Refr.' (clock time of apparent noon, before refraction): 9h53'15.8'', 16.7'', 17.9'', 23.7''.
- The gap between these two columns is 44.2, 45.0, 45.0 and 58.8 s. It is presumably an instrumental or index correction depending on t and p (perhaps from the Jacobi mark); the page does not show it.
- 'Wirk. d. Refr.' (effect of refraction on the hour angle): 6.1, 6.3, 6.6, 17.2 s.
- Subtracting gives noon clock times 9h53'9.7'', 10.4'', 11.3'', 6.5''.
- The mean is 9h53'9.5''.

On the refraction term (my explanation): refraction lifts the afternoon sun along the vertical, so the apparent hour angle is too small. The correction to t is Δt = R·sin q / cos δ, where R is the refraction and q the parallactic angle. Hence the noon clock time T − t must be reduced.
- With δ ≈ +13.8° and φ = 51.53°: t = 71.05° gives altitude ≈ 22.5°, R ≈ 2.4', sin q ≈ 0.636, so Δt ≈ 94'' of arc ≈ 6.3 s. Gauss has 6.1 s.
- t = 94.2° gives altitude ≈ 8.2°, R ≈ 6.4', so Δt ≈ 16.7 s. Gauss has 17.2 s.

At apparent noon, sidereal time equals the sun's right ascension, taken as 9h40'3.7''. This is plausible for 1815 Aug 16: solar longitude ≈ 143°, RA ≈ 9h40m. Clock error = 9h53'9.5'' − 9h40'3.7'' = +13'5.8''. The clock is fast on sidereal time by 13 min 5.8 s.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. The four subtractions, the mean (37.9/4 = 9.475 ≈ 9.5) and the final difference 13'5.8'' are all correct.

The correction of about 44–59 s between 'Uhr voraus' and 'Mittag ohne Refr.' is not shown and cannot be verified from this page. Its jump for the last observation suggests a term depending on hour angle (polar-axis or collimation error) rather than a constant index error.
The refraction effects agree with a modern estimate to about 0.2–0.5 s. Differences of this size can come from the refraction table or meteorological values used, so they are not real errors.

results.what: Clock correction of a sidereal clock from equatorial hour-angle observations of the sun, with refraction correction to the hour angle
results.modern_name: Time determination by hour angles (equatorial method); refraction in hour angle Δt = R sin q / cos δ
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practical astronomy of the 18th–19th century (Bouguer, Lalande, Bessel and others)

results.what: Hour-circle zero and 12h flip convention for a German equatorial mount
results.modern_name: Pier-side / meridian-flip convention for equatorial mounts

results.what: Survey of horizon obstructions in hour angle and polar distance; equatorial coordinates of a terrestrial mark (Jacobi tower)
results.modern_name: Horizon/obstruction mapping; azimuth mark for instrument orientation

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine observational bookkeeping from Gauss's setup of instruments at the new Göttingen observatory (1815–16): obstruction timings, a mount convention, a reference mark, and a standard clock-error reduction with refraction. Nothing here is mathematically novel.

checkable.asserts: Sun's altitude at hour angle 4h44m12s is about 22.5°
Refraction effect on hour angle ≈ 6.3 s of time (Gauss: 6.1 s), using R ≈ 144''
Polar distance of a north-meridian point at altitude 6.73° ≈ 44.8°, matching 44°56' for the Jacobi tower

transcription_corrections: Header 'Heliom.[?] in NW' is uncertain. The context is a sky-obstruction survey toward the NW, so the reading should be kept marked as doubtful.
'Wirkd. Refr.' is better read as 'Wirk. d. Refr.' (Wirkung der Refraction, effect of refraction).
The 'Uhr voraus' column entries 1,7 / 2,9 / 22,5 are abbreviations for 9h54'1.7'', 9h54'2.9'', 9h54'22.5''.
Under 'Sonne' the label 'U. Z.' is an abbreviation of uncertain meaning; the numbers 4h44'12'' etc. belong to the 'Stundenwinkel' column.
